title: Cluster architecture and the control plane
description: Ten questions on what each control plane component owns, how a request flows through the API server, and which failures map to which component.

questions.prompt: Which component decides which node a newly created Pod should run on?

options.text: kubelet
kube-scheduler
kube-controller-manager
kube-proxy
etcd

questions.explanation: kube-scheduler watches for Pods with an empty spec.nodeName, filters nodes that cannot run the Pod, scores the rest, and writes a Binding. The kubelet then starts the containers on the chosen node - it does not choose the node itself.

questions.prompt: Why should an etcd cluster always have an odd number of members?

options.text: Even numbers cause data corruption during writes
Raft requires a quorum of (n/2)+1, so an even count adds a member without improving fault tolerance
The API server can only connect to an odd number of endpoints
It is a soft convention with no technical effect

questions.explanation: A 3-member cluster tolerates 1 failure (quorum 2). A 4-member cluster also tolerates only 1 failure (quorum 3), so the extra member adds cost and write latency without improving availability.

questions.prompt: kube-apiserver is stopped. Existing application Pods are healthy and serving traffic. What happens?

options.text: All Pods are terminated immediately
Running Pods keep serving traffic, but no new scheduling or API changes are possible
Pods keep running but lose their network connectivity
The scheduler takes over the API server's responsibilities

questions.explanation: The data plane - kubelet, kube-proxy and your containers - keeps operating on the state it already has. Only the control plane's ability to make and accept changes is lost.

questions.prompt: In what order does the API server process an incoming request?

options.text: Authorisation, authentication, admission control, validation, persistence
Authentication, authorisation, admission control, validation, persistence
Admission control, authentication, authorisation, persistence, validation
Validation, authentication, authorisation, admission control, persistence

questions.explanation: Identity first (who are you - 401 on failure), then permission (may you do this - 403 on failure), then admission plugins and webhooks which may mutate or reject, then schema validation, and finally the write to etcd.

questions.prompt: On a kubeadm-built cluster, which components normally run as static Pods defined in /etc/kubernetes/manifests? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: kube-apiserver
etcd
kubelet
kube-scheduler
kube-controller-manager
CoreDNS

questions.explanation: The four control plane components run as static Pods managed by the kubelet. The kubelet itself is a systemd service (it cannot run itself as a Pod), and CoreDNS runs as an ordinary Deployment in kube-system.

questions.prompt: New Pods stay Pending indefinitely, while Pods that were already running are completely healthy. Which component is most likely broken?

options.text: kube-proxy
kube-scheduler
CoreDNS
The container runtime

questions.explanation: Pending means no node has been assigned. Assigning nodes is exactly the scheduler's job. If the scheduler is down, existing Pods are unaffected because they already have a nodeName.

questions.prompt: Immediately after 'kubeadm init', every node reports NotReady. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: etcd has not finished its initial election
No CNI network plugin has been installed yet
The nodes need to be manually labelled as Ready
The kubelet certificates have expired

questions.explanation: Without a CNI plugin the kubelet reports NetworkReady=false and the node condition stays NotReady. Installing Calico, Cilium or Flannel resolves it. 'kubectl describe node' shows the exact condition.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the Kubernetes reconciliation model are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: You write spec; the system writes status
Controllers continuously compare desired state to observed state
Deleting a Pod owned by a Deployment permanently reduces the replica count
Controllers watch the API server rather than polling etcd directly

questions.explanation: Only the API server talks to etcd. Deleting a Pod that a ReplicaSet owns creates a gap that the controller closes within seconds - the replica count is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Write the kubectl command that lists events in the current namespace sorted by their last timestamp.
questions.explanation: kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp is the single highest-value troubleshooting command: scheduling, image pull, probe and volume mount failures all surface here first.

questions.prompt: A node is NotReady. Write the systemd journal command that follows the kubelet logs on that node.
questions.explanation: The kubelet is a systemd unit, so its logs are in the journal rather than in kubectl. This is the first command to run on any NotReady node.
